cases.name: Alexandra Wynter
cases.about:
A tribute article in Chico State Today said, "Those who knew Alexandra Wynter describe her as naturally gifted and intelligent, deeply compassionate, a loyal and supportive friend, and a devoted dog mom. A senior biological sciences major, she carried a quiet warmth that made people feel cared for.

When Wynter came back to Chico State in fall 2024 as part of the University’s Second Start program after nearly six years away from the University, she was focused, driven, and ready.

She excelled immediately, earning strong grades as she worked toward her degree in cellular and molecular biology.

“She was confident, serious, and got things done quickly,” said Professor Robert Dubie, who taught Wynter in the lab portion of her “Hematology” course this semester. “She would leave class quickly after finishing her work, I could tell she was busy.”


Professor Nicole Kilian, who taught Wynter in the same course, remembered her as a brilliant, driven student whose friendly, engaged presence stood out in class. Early in the term, Wynter noticed she had been accidentally given extra points on an exam and immediately came back to correct the mistake—a small moment that, to Kilian, reflected her deep integrity.

Wynter’s long-term goal was to attend medical school—a path that reflected both her intellect and her desire to help others. Dubie said he had no doubt she would have succeeded.

“In class it was clear she was medically savvy and had real-world experience in the field,” said Dubie. “There’s no doubt in my mind she would have succeeded in medical school and been an outstanding physician.”

In addition to attending the University full time, Wynter worked at Enloe Health and planned to attend physician assistant school after graduating. Outside of school and work, she loved music and dancing, and she found joy and connection with her friends at music festivals. 

“Alexandra was one of the best people I’ve ever known—she didn’t have a mean bone in her body,” said Triana Slate, a close friend who knew Wynter since they were both 14 growing up in Lake Balboa. “She had this warmth, this calmness, that made you feel safe no matter what was going on. She always spoke up for people who didn’t have a voice. She was politically aware and passionate about voting, as well as humanitarian and environmental issues.”

Wynter chose to attend Chico State to try a different environment than Los Angeles and experience a college town. Over time, she fell in love with Chico’s nature and the sense of freedom it offered. During her first stint at the University, she served as the community connections director for Community Action Volunteers in Education, was a member of the Black Student Union, and volunteered extensively throughout the community.

At the height of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, she coordinated an effort with Chico City Councilmember Addison Winslow to provide aid to the unhoused community in Chico.

Friends say she was independent and private. She carved out a life in Chico that reflected her values—humility, focusing on helping the community, and connecting to the natural spaces she loved. She also traveled when she could, everywhere from Costa Rica to Mount Shasta, to deepen her love of nature and adventure.

“She loved her dog so much (who she named Wynter to deepen their connection). Some of my favorite moments with her were taking Wynter to Upper Bidwell and even the athletic fields at Chico State,” said Milissa Miller, Alexandra’s longtime friend in Chico. “She was the first person you would call when you needed help. She was there for me and let me stay with her when I needed to. She was always there to listen.”

Those closest to Alexandra say a sense of calm followed her everywhere—even into the most unpredictable moments. Slate remembers that Wynter had a remarkable way of staying grounded, no matter the circumstances.

“She always found herself in pretty interesting predicaments,” Slate said, laughing. “But she handled everything so calmly.”

One memory still makes her smile. At one of the last music festivals they attended together in the LA area, Wynter’s phone was stolen in a crowd of thousands. She became separated from her friend group, who frantically searched for her in the sea of people. They finally found her sitting cross-legged on the ground, unbothered.

“That was just her,” Slate said. “She never had a sour attitude. Even in chaos, she projected warmth and happiness.”

Miller said Wynter had a wonderful sense of humor but was sly about sneaking away just when a video for social media was about to be filmed. She would always say hello to Miller’s kids when she saw them in their neighborhood. She also introduced Miller to Oktoberfest at Sierra Nevada Brewing Co., where Wynter would have the time of her life singing, dancing, and eating at the annual festival.

Her friends, colleagues, and peers now mourn a life cut short, holding on to the warmth and compassion she shared so freely."
